0. FOREWORD

0.1 This Indian Standard ( First Revision ) was adopted by the Indian Standards Institution on 16 August 1984, after the draft finalized by the Natural and Synthetic Perfumery Materials Sectional Committee had Coal and Related Products Division been approved by the Petroleum, Council.
0.2 This standard was first published in 1955. The Sectional Committee responsible for its preparation felt that it should be revised with a view to bring it in line with trade practices in perfumery technology and also align with the quality level of the material currently manufactured and sold in the country. 0.3 Taking cognizance has been deleted in the has been included as it wet method of analysis deleted. Requirement of the material available in the country Grade 2 preset revision. Also gas chromatographic `analysis is being progressively used in the country and the for the determination of ester content has been of relative density has also been modified.

0.4 Linalyl acetate ( C11HZo02 ) is the acetate of the tertiary ally1 alcohol, linalool. It is extensively used in many floral compositions, ,eau-decolognes, in the manufacture of artificial oils of lavender and bergamot and employed to a-limited extent in soaps and cosmetics. 0.4.1 Linalyl acetate synthetically is obtained by total synthetic route ex acetylene or isoprene via dehydrolinalool and also from ,8 pinene via myrcene and myrcene hydrochloride. 0.5 Linalyl acetate occurs in nature in oils of bergamot, lavender, petitgrain, ylang, ylang coriander and many others. It is also known as 3,7dimethy l- 1,6-otadien-3-yl acetate,

3

IS : 3180 - 1984 0.5.1 It is also obtained from linalool by acetylation several hours at controlled temperatures. It is represented structural formula:

The number of significant places retained in the rounded off value should be the same as that of the specified value in this standard.

4. PACKING

AND MARKING

4.1 Packing - The material shall be packed in amber-coloured glass or other air-tight, preferably opaque containers such as tin-lined or aluminium permitting a minimum of air space. Good quality lacquer-lined drums may also be used. 4.1.1 The materia1 shall be protected and dry place. 4.2 Marking - Each following informations: container from light and stored in a legibly and indelibly
cool

shall bear

the

a) Name of the material; b) Name of the manufacturer and any; c) Net mass of the material; and d) Batch number. 4.2.1 The particular source from which the material shall be marked on each container. 4.2.2 Mark. The containers may also be marked has been obtained Certification his recognized trade-mark, if

with the ISI

NOTE - The use of the IS1 Certification Mark is governed by the provisions of the Indian Standards Institution ( Certification Marks) Act and the Rules and Regulations made thereunder. The ISI ,Mark on products covered by an Indian Standard conveys the assurance that they have been produced to comply with the requirements of that standard under a well-defined system of inspection, testing and quality control which is devised and supervised by IS1 ando perated by the producer. ISI marked products are also continuously checked by IS1 for conformity to that standard as a further safeguard. Details of conditions, under which a licence for the use of the IS1 Certification Mark may be granted to manufacturers or processors, may be obtained from the Indian Standards Institution.

GAS CHROMATOGRAPHIC ANALYSIS FOR DETERMINATION OF LINALYL ACETATE A-O. GENERAL A-O.1 The chromatographic
conditions given here are for guidance only.

A-O.2 Outline of the Method - A sample of the material is dissolved in a suitable solvent ( for example, cychohexane and diethyl ether ) and is injected into the gas chromatograph where it is carried by the carrier gas from one end of the column to the other. During its movement, constituents of the sample undergo distribution at different rates and
*Specification for water for general laboratory use ( second w&ion ).

7

IS : 3180 - 1984 The separated constituents ultimately get separated from one another. emerge from the end of the column one after another and are detected by suitable means whose response is related to the amount of a specfiic component leaving the column.

A-l.APPARATUS
A-l.1 Any suitable for used. 8

IS : 3180 - 1984 A-2. PROCEDURE A-2.1 Conduct the flow of the carrier
gas and inject the sample ( dissolved in the suitable solvent ) at inject port where it is vapourized and well mixed with the carrier. This is led into the chromatographic column wherein vaporized constituents of the sample are separated out by virtue of their differing interaction with the stationary phase. As the differen constituents pass through the detector, they give signals corresponding to the amount of particular constituent leaving the column. The detector signals, on transmission to the recorder, plotst he chart. From the specific area uvder various peaks corresponding to specific constituents, the quantities of different constituents are determined. NOTE - For the separation to be efficient, it is necessary that the column is
maintained at the temperature tion of the constituents. suggested throughout the time required for the resolu-

IS t 3180 - 1984 A-3. CALCULATION A-3.1 Area Measurement ( seeNote 1 ) - Since normal peaks approximate a triangle the area is measured by multiplying the peak height times the width of half height. The normal peak base is not taken since large This technique deviations may be observed due to tailing or adsorption. is rapid, simple and fairly accurate when peaks are symmetrical and of reasonable width. A-3.2 Area Normalization ( seeNote 2 ) - By normalizing, it is meant, calculating the percentage composition by measuring the area of each and dividing the individual areas by total area, for example, Percentage of A = Area of A -Total area

x 100

NOTE1 - Other methods of area measurement namely, Triangulation, Disc integrator and Electronic digital integrator if fixed with GLC machine would be of great advantage. NOTE2 - Internal standardiiation can be used if pure appropriate internal standard is available. This method is known as relative or indirect calibration.

APPENDIX

B

[ Table I, Item ( vii ) ]
TEST FOR FREEDOM FROM CHLORINATED B-O. GENERAL B-O.1 Outline of the Method - Absence of even a transient green colour, when the material is ignited on a copper gauze in a non-luminous flame is used for determining freedom from chlorinated compounds. B-l. APPARATUS COMPOUNDS

B-l.1 Copper-wire bent at one end to which a strip of 850-micron copper gauze 15 mm wide and 50 mm long is attached. B-l.2 Dropper capable of giving good non-luminous flame. 10

B-l.3 Bunsen Burner -

1s t 3186- 1984 B-2. PROCEDURE B-2.1 Place the copper strip in non-luminous flame of the Bunsen burner Cool the gauze and until it glows without imparting a green colour. Cool the gauze repeatedly ignite'it until an oxide coating had formed. and add 2 drops of the sample by means of a dropper, permitting it to burn in the air, Again cool and add 2 more drops of the test material and burn as before. Continue the procedure until 6 drops have been ignited. Hold the gauze in the outer edge of the non-luminous flame whose height has been adjusted to about 40 mm. B-2.1.1 The material shall be deemed to have passed the test if the flame is free of even a transient green colour.
